subject: printing variable names in error messages

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: printing variable names in error messages
parts:
On 10/2/12 7:08 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:

> As an aside, Bob, how hard would be it to catch transformation
> exceptions when they're thrown in the model code and report the
> variable name they arose on? Alternatively could we propogate the
> model level expressions and/or variable names down through the calls
> in case exceptions are thrown? The hardest part of debugging this was
> figuring out exactly which matrix was failing the symmetry test which
> required the use of gdb.

In case you didn't see the other message on stan-users, yes, we could do
that. We'd need to change every function to take in extra
arguments for the function name. Or, maybe it'd be enough
to pass in line numbers from the source? (Not so helpful for
all those writing models as strings in R.)

We should probably add error checking to the basic functions,
too, like log and arctan and what not.

- Bob

Sorry.  I missed this while I was writing the reply to the users list.  Here is what I said there;

--

For exceptions in the model this would be problematic.  However,
parameters which fail their constraint checks in write_data/write_csv
should be done more easily....Actually, I just looked and it's already
kind of implemented but the check_cov_matrix function doesn't pass
along the variable name and just substitutes "y".  I just pushed a fix
for this for symmetry and positive definiteness but fixing the size
checks is more involved.

That said, I was thinking that more generally when the constraint
check code is generated it could be wrapped in a try {} catch {} block
which would add the variable name to the error message avoiding the
need to propagate things down at all.

--

Actually, I think that strategy could even work for the model section.  Each "line" of the .stan model file gets translated to a block of C++ code which can get wrapped in a try {} catch{} block which could at least add the line number to the exception message.  Maybe even a stack trace if it's available.  It's not perfect but is a small(er) change to the model compilation code which I think would greatly improve the user experience and our debugging ability/efficiency.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] printing variable names in error messages
parts:
Ok, unit tests passed so I pushed the changes. This should give users
more useful error messages in some cases. Plus, I think we could use
the same approach to give us better error messages in log_prob and
elsewhere.

Basically where it used to produce code like this:

stan::math::check_cov_matrix(function__,S_d,"S_d");

stanc now produces code like this:

try { stan::math::check_cov_matrix(function__,S_d,"S_d"); } catch
(std::domain_error e) { throw std::domain_error(std::string("Invalid
value of S_d: ") + std::string(e.what())); };

The error messages could be made a bit more useful by including array
indexes where individual elements are test, but this is at least a
start.

Cheers,
Marcus

Neat. I'd thought about doing something like this for
every statement we call so we could identify line numbers.

From what I see, it looks like you're checking the transformed
variables. What I haven't been able to figure out is how to
do something like this inside the density functions where we
currently just throw generic domain_error exceptions.

I'd also very much like to figure out how to make sure
we don't duplicate tests. This is part of the goal of
Ben's working on a new data structure for covariance matrices
with caching for things like the Cholesky factors.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Help with multivariate ordered logistic model
parts:
On 10/2/12 8:40 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> ... mdivide_left(A,b) and mdivide_right(b,A) will give you A^-1
> *b and b*A^-1 respectively. See also mdivide_left_tri if you're using
> the cholesky factors. I'm not sure if they're exposed to the
> modelling language yet. Let me know if you need them and they're not
> and I can maybe get that cleaned up.

We used Matlab notation,

mdivide_left(A,b) is (A \ b)

mdivide_right(b,A) is (b / A)

We didn't add mdivide_left_tri yet, but I'll add that
to the function_signatures and doc as soon as I finish
this e-mail.

- Bob

parts:
On Wed, Oct 3, 2012 at 1:45 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:


On 10/3/12 12:38 AM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
Ok, unit tests passed so I pushed the changes.  This should give users
more useful error messages in some cases.  Plus, I think we could use
the same approach to give us better error messages in log_prob and
elsewhere.

Basically where it used to produce code like this:

stanc now produces code like this:

try { stan::math::check_cov_matrix(function__,S_d,"S_d"); } catch
(std::domain_error e) { throw std::domain_error(std::string("Invalid
value of S_d: ") + std::string(e.what())); };

The error messages could be made a bit more useful by including array
indexes where individual elements are test, but this is at least a
start.

Neat.   I'd thought about doing something like this for
every statement we call so we could identify line numbers.

I looked into that a bit today and it should be pretty simple.  The only catch was that I couldn't figure out how to get the parser to associate the line numbers with the statements.  I start going crazy when I look too deeply at the boost spirit parser stuff.

From what I see, it looks like you're checking the transformed
variables.  What I haven't been able to figure out is how to
do something like this inside the density functions where we
currently just throw generic domain_error exceptions.

If stan::gm::sample and stan::gm::assignment included the model line numbers which generated them I think this would be relatively straightforward.  It's just a matter of generating the added try/catch blocks which I was able to figure out how to do without too much trouble.  That added code could also check for nonfinite lp__ and give an early exit with an informative error message.  Again, all of that is pretty easy once we have line numbers in the sample and assignment structs.

I'd also very much like to figure out how to make sure
we don't duplicate tests.  This is part of the goal of
Ben's working on a new data structure for covariance matrices
with caching for things like the Cholesky factors.

Most tests don't hurt that badly with the SPD test being one which does.  One way to make it a lot faster would be to specialize the test for matrices of vars and have it copy the values to a matrix of doubles and test on that instead.  That way we don't create tons of vars for the cholesky factor which are never needed for differentiation.

Cheers,
Marcus
